4	Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

6	Part of #35

8	## Why
9	
10	`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
11	without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
12	Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
13	providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
14	shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
15	casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
16	that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
17	written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
18	confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.
19	
20	The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
21	to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
22	in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
23	of it.
24	
25	## What to do
26	
27	Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
28	`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
29	unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
30	schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
31	providers.
32	
33	Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
34	not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
35	resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.
36	
37	A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
38	so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
39	`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
40	generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
41	it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
42	there is no opt-out flag.
43	
44	Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.
45	
46	## Acceptance criteria
47	
48	- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
49	      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
50	      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
51	- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
52	      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
53	      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
54	      count is `0`
55	- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
56	      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
57	      exactly once
58	- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
59	      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
60	      **not** contain the offending value
61	- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
62	      that the thrown message names the tool
63	- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
64	      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
65	- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
66	- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
67	      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
68	      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
69	      round
70	- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
71	      pinned by a test
72	- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
73	      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
74	      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
75	      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
76	      containing that field's value
77	- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
78	      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
79	      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
80	      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
81	- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
82	      `devDependencies`, and
83	      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
84	- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
85	      merely present
86	- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
87	      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
88	      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
89	      returned to the model rather than thrown
90	- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
91	      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
92	      properties pass through unmodified
93	- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
94	      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
95	      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
96	      bump is MINOR
97	- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
98	      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist

100	      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
101	- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
102	      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
103	      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
104	- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
105	      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface
106	
107	## Tech notes
108	
109	Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
110	`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
111	WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends

113	`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.
114

116	class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
117	direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
118	throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
119	evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
120	valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
121	owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
122	authorization model); retry, timeout
123	and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
124	written against this contract later.

# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

6	> providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model.

8	**Strategy: `direct`** — `ToolRegistry.register`, `ToolRegistry.execute` and `createChatOrchestrator` already expose the exact entry points this ticket changes, so the acceptance tests call them directly today and fail because schema compilation and input validation are absent.
9	
10	## Done when these pass
11	
12	- [ ] **rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor** — `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against `inputSchema`, returns a `ToolResponse` naming the missing required property, and does not invoke the executor.
13	  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`
14	
15	- [ ] **rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs** — `ToolRegistry.execute` rejects a property with the wrong JSON Schema type without calling the executor, names the failing field path and expected type in `result`, and omits the offending property value from both `result` and emitted log lines.
16	  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`
17	
18	- [ ] **throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled** — `ToolRegistry.register` compiles a static `ToolDefinition`'s `inputSchema` once at registration time and throws synchronously naming the tool when the schema is invalid.
19	  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

# Definition of Done

> `ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
> without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
> Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
> providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model.

**Strategy: `direct`** — `ToolRegistry.register`, `ToolRegistry.execute` and `createChatOrchestrator` already expose the exact entry points this ticket changes, so the acceptance tests call them directly today and fail because schema compilation and input validation are absent.

## Done when these pass

- [ ] **rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor** — `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against `inputSchema`, returns a `ToolResponse` naming the missing required property, and does not invoke the executor.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs** — `ToolRegistry.execute` rejects a property with the wrong JSON Schema type without calling the executor, names the failing field path and expected type in `result`, and omits the offending property value from both `result` and emitted log lines.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled** — `ToolRegistry.register` compiles a static `ToolDefinition`'s `inputSchema` once at registration time and throws synchronously naming the tool when the schema is invalid.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round** — `createChatOrchestrator` feeds a schema-rejected tool call's `ToolResponse.result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` without invoking the executor on the invalid call, allowing the model to retry with valid arguments and complete the turn.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

## Facets

- [x] Add `ajv` to `dependencies` in `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (`strict: false`, `validateFormats: false`, no coercion, no defaults, no injected `additionalProperties: false`) and bump the package version `MINOR`.
- [x] Compile static `ToolDefinition.inputSchema` at `ToolRegistry.register` time (throwing an error naming the tool on invalid schemas) and cache compiled validators for function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` schemas by schema object reference (`WeakMap`).
- [x] Validate `input` in `ToolRegistry.execute` before invoking the executor, returning a `ToolResponse` (`{result}`) that names failing field paths and expected types/required fields without echoing or logging offending values, and add the one-line doc comment pointing at `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`.
- [ ] Add unit tests in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` and `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts`, link the remaining statements in `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, and update `example/weather-tool.ts`, `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md`, `.specify/spec.md`, `adrs/ADR-002-response-validation.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md`.
- [ ] Pin that a static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled once and reused across repeated `execute` calls (ticket criterion; `spec.md` statement "compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call" is still uncited — needs an observable seam for the compile count, no test can read it off the current surface).

## Out of scope

- Output validation and domain sanity checks (covered by ADR-002), MCP tool-server discovery and proxying (#42), per-tool authorization or `beforeToolCall` hooks (#40), retry/timeout/rate-limiting around tool execution, and concrete tool implementations.

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Manual runs: re-checking a branch against a moved main, or confirming a gate after
  # changing one, without pushing an empty commit.
  workflow_dispatch:
  # An advisory published after a merge is invisible until someone opens a pull request, and this
  # repository can go days without one. Monday 07:00 UTC; only `build-chain` answers it.
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * 1'

# Every job here only reads the checkout; the repo default is write.
permissions:
  contents: read

# A newer push to the same branch supersedes an in-flight run. main is exempt:
# every commit there should have its own recorded result.

  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }}

jobs:
  verify:
    name: Verify
    # The scheduled run exists for the dependency audit; re-running the suite on an unchanged
    # tree every Monday would report nothing new.
    if: github.event_name != 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
          # Full history, not for this job but for the spec anchor check below:
          # it resolves cited content from
          # origin/main, which a shallow clone cannot serve.
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@820762786026740c76f36085b0efc47a31fe5020 # v7.0.0
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: npm

      # --ignore-scripts so `prepare` does not build on install: what a lifecycle script
      # runs is out of this workflow's control, and the Build step below is where a broken
      # compile should be reported. Type check catches it earlier still.
      - name: Install
        run: npm ci --ignore-scripts

      # Every `npm run` step below is one link of the `verify` script in
      # package.json, in the same order - scripts/verify-script.test.ts holds
      # the two together - and kept as separate steps so a red run names the
      # gate that failed rather than a single opaque command.
      - name: Type check
        run: npm run typecheck

      # example/ is outside tsconfig.json's rootDir, so nothing checked the one
      # file the README and the guide are written against.
      - name: Type check the example
        run: npm run typecheck:example

      - name: Lint (--max-warnings 0)
        run: npm run eslint

      # Reports, never blocks. The one rule it runs is `warn`, so the step exits
      # 0 on its own and carries no continue-on-error: a non-zero exit here now
      # means the config itself broke, and that should fail. Its findings render
      # as warning annotations rather than failures, which is what a report on a
      # passing check should look like.
      #
      # require-statement-links counts spec statements with no test behind them.
      # Most of what it reports needs a test written rather than a line changed,
      # so the count is meant to be visible on every run and to fall over time.
      # Its test-side mirror, require-spec-link, is satisfied and gates in the
      # Lint step above. Never add a rule here to escape a red gate -
      # eslint.config.backlog.mjs says what belongs.
      - name: Spec traceability backlog (report)
        run: npm run lint:backlog

      - name: Format check
        run: npm run prettier:check

      # Runs the whole suite and fails it on the committed coverage floor in
      # jest.config.js, so this is the test gate rather than an extra pass.
      - name: Test (with coverage floor)
        run: npm run test:coverage

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

      # Anchors drift silently: a cited file gaining or losing lines above the
      # cited one leaves the link pointing at different content, and the spec
      # still reads as cited. Resolves content at origin/main, which the
      # fetch-depth: 0 above exists to provide. A red check is fixed by running
      # `node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs` and committing the result.
      - name: Spec anchor check
        run: node scripts/repoint-spec-anchors.mjs --check origin/main

      # A citation counts as coverage only in its statement's trailing
      # parenthetical; one written mid-statement is dropped by the Lore job in silence,
      # so the spec reads as cited while its coverage is zero. A red check is
      # fixed by moving the link to the end of its statement, never by deleting
      # it (AGENTS.md § Spec Test Links).
      # Every fenced typescript block in the three documented files is generated
      # from source; hand transcription is what produced the defects this catches.
      - name: Documented code blocks
        run: npm run docs:check

      # Three rules that held only because somebody remembered them: a path in prose that resolves,
      # a spike that says it is a spike, and an example region inside the EU.
      - name: Documented paths resolve
        run: npm run docs:check-paths

      - name: Spike documents carry a status block
        run: npm run docs:check-spikes

      - name: Documented regions
        run: npm run check:regions

# Lore test-command interface (lore_list_tests / lore_run_test).
# Written for this repo's Jest suite rather than adapted from the Vitest
# equivalent for a Vitest suite: the report shapes happen to match, but the

  name: HAL Engine Jest suite

    on every pull request in .github/workflows/ci.yml as the "Test" step.
    Selectors are "<repo-relative-file>::<full test name>" as emitted by the
    list command. Jest has no dry-run, so the list command executes the suite
    once with --json and derives every name from the report; it deliberately
    tolerates a red suite, since listing must not depend on the tests passing.
    The run command selects one test with --runTestsByPath plus an anchored,
    regex-escaped -t, and treats a selector that matches nothing as a failure
    rather than a green run of an empty suite. Neither command builds first:
    no test here reads dist/.
  list: node scripts/lore-list-tests.mjs
  run: node scripts/lore-run-test.mjs "{selector}"

content.content:
# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | In Progress          |

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46), [validated by: rejects a wrong-typed field naming the path and expected type but not the offending value](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L70)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults ([validated by: passes an undeclared extra property through to the executor unchanged and calls it once](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L47)).
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake ([validated by: still throws Unknown tool for an unregistered name](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L90)).

## Schema compilation and caching

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).
- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema`.
- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules ([validated by: validates each call against the schema the definition function returns for that call](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L19)).

## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery

- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).

Base directory for this skill: /var/tmp/loop-bench/runs/02e68b283c3a/home-3/.claude/skills/tdd-loop

This is the authoritative copy of Lore's TDD contract for agent runs. It is checked
into the Lore repo at `apps/mcp-server/agent-skills/skills/tdd-loop/` and served to
pods by the gateway's `/skills` registry.

You run the three phases yourself, in order, in one pass. Do not skip a phase and do
not run two facets in one round.

## The three laws

1. Do not write production code unless it is to make a failing test pass.
2. Do not write more of a unit test than is sufficient to fail — a compile or import
   failure counts.
3. Do not write more production code than is sufficient to make the currently failing
   test pass.

## Phase 1 — RED

Detect the toolchain from the project (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `pyproject.toml`,
`Cargo.toml`, `pom.xml`, `Gemfile`, `mix.exs`, `Makefile`, CI config) and mirror the
conventions already in the repo's tests — framework, directory, file suffix, assertion
style. Assume nothing about the language.

**The one-facet rule.** Name the single smallest behaviour that moves you forward. If
the behaviour you were handed would force more than one new facet, write the test for
the smallest facet only and report the leftovers rather than growing the round.

Write **exactly one** test. Run it. Confirm it fails **for the reason you expect** —
the behaviour is absent, not the import path typo'd or a fixture missing. A test you
did not run is not a red bar, it is a guess.

If a behaviour would not change the code under test at all, say so and write nothing.
A test that forces no change is not worth writing.

### No mocks, no stubs

Design every test to exercise pure logic with real values — value in, value out, not
interactions. A facet that seems to *require* a double is a design signal: the real
problem is an unmanaged side effect, not the absence of a mock. Pick a facet that is
testable without doubles, and note that the production code should push the I/O to the
edges so the pure core is directly testable.

- Stubbed lookup → pure function on a value. `discountFor(user)` taking a real `User`,
  not `discountFor(userId)` fetching one behind a `UserRepository` stub.
- Interaction mock → assert on a returned value. Have the core return the intent and
  assert `notificationsFor(order)`; sending happens at the edge.
- Clock/RNG stub → inject the value. `isExpired(deadline, now)`, both plain values.

A true collaborator boundary that must eventually be pinned down is a separate
**contract test**, never an ad-hoc mock sprinkled into a unit test.

### Test naming

The principle is language-agnostic; the surface form follows the language.

- Short, clear, scannable. The name carries the expected behaviour **and** the tested
  data — never the implementation.
- No "should".
- Apply the *ask-why* check: a name that does not answer why the test exists is a
  structural name, not an intent-revealing one.
- Include the context only when the enclosing suite does not already establish it.

Good: `returns 0 for an empty list`, `returns I for 1`, `throws RangeError for 0`.
Bad: `should return zero`, `test sum`, `works correctly`.

## Phase 2 — GREEN

Write the fewest lines that turn the bar green. No extra features, no speculative
generality, no refactoring yet.

**Kent Beck's green-bar strategies:**

- *Obvious implementation* — when the real code is trivial and unmistakable, write it.
- *Fake it* — when it is not, return a constant and let a later test replace constants
  with variables.
- *Triangulate* — leave generalization to the NEXT test. Do not guess the general
  solution now.

Run the tests you are working against — the one you just wrote plus the acceptance
tests that define done — by naming their files. Never the repository's whole suite:
CI runs that on every push, and the pod's Bash hook refuses a bare `npm test` or
`vitest run` with no path. All of what you run must pass.

**Never edit the test to make it pass.** If the test is wrong, say so and stop; that is
a finding, not a green bar.

### Where code goes

Never create code in catch-all `utils` / `misc` / `helpers` / `common` / `shared` /
`lib` modules. Place and name code by the domain concept it serves — discount logic in
`pricing/`, not `utils/calc.ts`. When no home exists, create a domain-named module,
never a generic bucket.

### Naming

Meaningful but concise — one to three words (`pendingOrders`, `isContainer`,
`retryCount`). No single letters except trivial loop indices; no `temp`/`data`/`x`; no
sprawling four-plus-word names. Name by role: `rawInput`, `normalized`.

## Phase 3 — REFACTOR

The bar is green. Improve the design without changing behaviour, and fit the new code
into the surrounding architecture. The suite stays green throughout.

**Duplication is duplicated knowledge, not just duplicated text.** Hunt for and
collapse: the same business rule expressed two ways, a constant or validation
re-derived in two places, parallel structures encoding one concept, a domain concept
named differently across modules, the same idea living in both code and a test.

Refactor **both** production and test code. Test refactoring counts: collapsing
duplicated tests into one parameterized test, removing now-subsumed tests, extracting
shared setup, clarifying names. Behaviour coverage must not shrink.

### The Simple Design Dynamo

Reuse is a **result** of removing duplication, never a prediction. Never extract because
something "might" be reused. For each candidate, in order:

1. Remove the duplication — collapse the copies into one. The reusable shape only
   becomes visible after the duplication is gone.
2. Separate what varies from what stays the same.
3. Extract a template — the algorithm steps with explicit variation points.
4. Name each operation concretely. **If a step cannot be named, the variation is not
   understood yet — stop and look.**
5. Parameterize the details — lift literals into arguments. Generic logic in code,
   specific values in data passed in.

This loops: removing duplication creates structures → you name them → better names
raise cohesion → higher cohesion makes the next, bigger duplication visible.

**Rule of three.** Two copies = notice, and remove the duplication *in place*. Promote
to a shared module only on the third genuinely similar case. Lifting on the second copy
couples unrelated callers and is harder to undo than the duplication was.

### Reveal intent

For any name you touch, ask "why does this exist / what is it really?" — the name must
answer that, not describe the mechanism. A function name containing "and"
(`parseAndStore`) is two responsibilities; split it. Improve names iteratively:
nonsense → structurally accurate → intent-revealing.

### Fewest elements

Inline indirection that does not pull its weight — a wrapper that only forwards. Apply
"too simple to break": never add a test for trivial composition of already-trusted
parts. Reject premature abstraction.

### Refactor discipline — this is where rounds go wrong

- **Never change production code and test code in the same step.** Each step touches
  only tests or only production code, then run the suite to green before the next.
  Changing both at once means a green bar no longer proves the refactor was safe.
- One target per step, always.
- **If a step turns the suite red, revert that step** rather than chasing the failure.
- Grep for existing abstractions to reuse before inventing new ones.
- May move or extract code and create files, but never add behaviour or expand scope
  beyond the current test.

### Out-of-scope smells

While you have the context loaded, note architecture and code smells you spot that are
**unrelated** to the current round — god objects, leaky abstractions, missing seams,
dead code. **Do not fix them**; that blows the round's scope. Collect them as
`future_improvements`: location + smell + one-line suggested fix. Report them; act on
none.

## Ending the round

Commit and push per the delivery contract in your task instructions — in a pod, the
work dies with the container otherwise. Commit only on green; a red suite is never
pushed.

Report: the facet you closed, the facet you would take next, the post-refactor test
result, and the `future_improvements` list.

# Adding a New Tool

Tools let the AI model fetch data or perform actions during a conversation. When the model decides it needs information (like weather data or a database lookup), it invokes a tool by name, the server executes it, and the result feeds back into the conversation.

Adding a new tool takes two steps: define it and register it. The rest is automatic -- the orchestrator passes tools to the AI provider, and the client already knows how to render any tool entry.

## Step 1: Create the tool file

Create a new file in `src/orchestration/tools/`. Each tool exports two things:

- A **`ToolDefinition`** describing the tool's name, purpose, and input schema
- A **`ToolExecutor`** function that runs the tool and returns a JSON string

Here is a complete example:

<!-- doc-block: example/weather-tool.ts#weather-tool -->
```typescript
import type {ToolDefinition, ToolExecutor} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';

export const weatherTool: ToolDefinition = {
  name: 'get_weather',
  description:
    'Get the current weather for a location.\n\n' +
    'Use this tool when the user:\n' +
    '* Asks about weather or temperature\n' +
    '* Wants to know conditions at a specific place\n' +
    '* Needs a forecast for planning\n\n' +
    'Returns temperature, conditions, humidity, and wind speed.',
  promptInstructions:
    'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +
    'Call this for questions like "What is the weather in Berlin?" or "Is it raining in Tokyo?"',
  examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],
  inputSchema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      location: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'The city name or location to look up.',
      },
      units: {
        type: 'string',
        enum: ['celsius', 'fahrenheit'],
        description: 'Temperature units. Defaults to celsius.',
      },
    },
    required: ['location'],
  },
};

export const executeWeather: ToolExecutor = async input => {
  const location = (input.location as string) || 'Unknown';
  const units = (input.units as string) || 'celsius';

  // Replace with a real API call. `input` is untrusted: inputSchema shapes what the model sends, it does not enforce it.
  const result = {
    location,
    temperature: 18,
    units,
    conditions: 'Partly cloudy',
    humidity: 65,
    windSpeed: 12,
    windUnit: 'km/h',
  };

  return JSON.stringify(result);
};
```

### Writing a good tool description

The `description` field is what the AI model reads to decide when to use the tool. Be specific:

- List the situations where the tool should be used ("Use this tool when...")
- Describe what the tool returns
- Give example queries if it helps

The more precise the description, the better the model's judgment about when to invoke it.

### Adding prompt instructions

The optional `promptInstructions` field provides guidance that gets included in the AI's system prompt. Unlike `description` (which is part of the tool schema sent to the AI provider), `promptInstructions` appears in the system prompt text itself, giving higher-level behavioral rules about when and how to use the tool.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
promptInstructions:
  'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +
  'Call this for questions like "What is the weather in Berlin?" or "Is it raining in Tokyo?"',
```

The `ToolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` method collects these from all registered tools, and the `PromptBuilder` assembles them into the system prompt automatically. If you don't provide `promptInstructions`, the tool still works -- it just won't have explicit guidance in the system prompt.

Use `promptInstructions` for:
- Short, actionable rules about when to call the tool
- Critical behavioral constraints (e.g., "MUST call this for every weather question")
- Example queries that help the model match user intent

Don't duplicate what's already in `description` -- keep `promptInstructions` focused on behavioral rules rather than describing inputs/outputs.

### Adding example prompts

The optional `examplePrompts` field provides example queries that are shown to users in the chat interface as clickable suggestions. These are sent to the client in the WebSocket `connected` message and persist throughout the conversation.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],
```

The `ToolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` method collects and flattens these from all registered tools. They are computed once at server startup and included in every new WebSocket connection's `connected` message.

Guidelines:
- Write prompts as natural user questions, not technical descriptions
- Keep them short and specific -- they appear as pill-shaped buttons in the UI
- 1-2 prompts per tool is enough; the total across all tools should stay manageable
- Use realistic terminology relevant to your application domain

### Defining the input schema

The `inputSchema` follows [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) format. The model uses this to construct the correct input.

- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields
- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these
- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)

### Writing the executor

A `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

The optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.

- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message
- Cast input fields from `unknown` to their expected types
- Handle missing or unknown input gracefully (return a reasonable default or error message)

For tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.

## Step 2: Register the tool

Open `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:

<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->
```typescript
import {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';

// ... existing registrations ...

toolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);
```

That is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry looks up the executor by name and runs it.

## What happens automatically

Once a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:

**On the backend:**

- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider
- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`
- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`
- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)

**On the client:**

- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields
- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**
- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**
- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives

## File reference

| File | What it contains |
|------|-----------------|
| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |
| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |
| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |

```typescript
    required: ['location'],
  },
};

export const executeWeather: ToolExecutor = async input => {
  const location = (input.location as string) || 'Unknown';
  const units = (input.units as string) || 'celsius';

  // Replace with a real API call. `input` is untrusted: inputSchema shapes what the model sends, it does not enforce it.
  const result = {
    location,
    temperature: 18,
    units,
    conditions: 'Partly cloudy',
    humidity: 65,
    windSpeed: 12,
    windUnit: 'km/h',
  };

  return JSON.stringify(result);
};
```

### Writing a good tool description

The `description` field is what the AI model reads to decide when to use the tool. Be specific:

- List the situations where the tool should be used ("Use this tool when...")
- Describe what the tool returns
- Give example queries if it helps

The more precise the description, the better the model's judgment about when to invoke it.

### Adding prompt instructions

The optional `promptInstructions` field provides guidance that gets included in the AI's system prompt. Unlike `description` (which is part of the tool schema sent to the AI provider), `promptInstructions` appears in the system prompt text itself, giving higher-level behavioral rules about when and how to use the tool.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
promptInstructions:
  'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +
  'Call this for questions like "What is the weather in Berlin?" or "Is it raining in Tokyo?"',
```

The `ToolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` method collects these from all registered tools, and the `PromptBuilder` assembles them into the system prompt automatically. If you don't provide `promptInstructions`, the tool still works -- it just won't have explicit guidance in the system prompt.

Use `promptInstructions` for:
- Short, actionable rules about when to call the tool
- Critical behavioral constraints (e.g., "MUST call this for every weather question")
- Example queries that help the model match user intent

Don't duplicate what's already in `description` -- keep `promptInstructions` focused on behavioral rules rather than describing inputs/outputs.

### Adding example prompts

The optional `examplePrompts` field provides example queries that are shown to users in the chat interface as clickable suggestions. These are sent to the client in the WebSocket `connected` message and persist throughout the conversation.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],
```

The `ToolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` method collects and flattens these from all registered tools. They are computed once at server startup and included in every new WebSocket connection's `connected` message.

Guidelines:
- Write prompts as natural user questions, not technical descriptions
- Keep them short and specific -- they appear as pill-shaped buttons in the UI
- 1-2 prompts per tool is enough; the total across all tools should stay manageable
- Use realistic terminology relevant to your application domain

### Defining the input schema

The `inputSchema` follows [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) format. The model uses this to construct the correct input.

- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields
- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these
- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)

### Writing the executor

A `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

The optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.

- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message
- Cast input fields from `unknown` to their expected types
- Handle missing or unknown input gracefully (return a reasonable default or error message)

For tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.

## Step 2: Register the tool

Open `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:

<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->
```typescript
import {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';

// ... existing registrations ...

toolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);
```

That is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry looks up the executor by name and runs it.

## What happens automatically

Once a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:

**On the backend:**

- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider
- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`
- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`
- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)

**On the client:**

- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields
- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**
- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**
- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives

## File reference

| File | What it contains |
|------|-----------------|
| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |
| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |
| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |

# Changelog

All notable changes to `@re-cinq/hal-engine` are documented here.

The format is [Keep a Changelog 1.1.0](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and this project adheres to
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html). Entries are written for somebody installing the
package, not for somebody reading this repository's commit log.

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- Tool input is validated against the tool's declared `inputSchema` before its executor runs. A call the schema
  rejects returns a tool result naming what was wrong — the missing required property or the expected type of a
  mistyped field — instead of reaching your executor, so the model reads the rejection and corrects the call on its
  next round. Valid input passes through untouched: extra properties still reach the executor, and nothing is
  coerced, defaulted or additionally forbidden. If your executor used to hand-validate its input it now receives
  only input the schema accepts; a tool that relied on seeing malformed input to produce its own error message
  stops seeing it.
- A tool whose `inputSchema` is not valid JSON Schema is rejected when it is registered, with an error naming the
  tool, so a broken schema fails at startup rather than mid-conversation.

## [0.3.0] - 2026-09-17

### Changed

- `HalEngineConfig.orchestrator.hooks` now carries a JSDoc comment. The field already shipped
  in `0.2.x`; the comment makes the lifecycle-hook seam discoverable from the published type
  declarations so editors surface it on hover without a trip to the README.

# Tool Input Validation

| Field  | Value                |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| Issue  | re-cinq/HALEngine#37 |
| Status | In Progress          |

Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.

## Validation at execute time

- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L16)).
- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L46), [validated by: rejects a wrong-typed field naming the path and expected type but not the offending value](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L70)).
- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults ([validated by: passes an undeclared extra property through to the executor unchanged and calls it once](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L47)).
- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake ([validated by: still throws Unknown tool for an unregistered name](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L90)).

## Schema compilation and caching

- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L94), [validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L4)).
- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema`.
- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules ([validated by: validates each call against the schema the definition function returns for that call](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L19)).

## Orchestrator tool-loop recovery

- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L112)).

A `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

The optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.

- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message

```typescript
import {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';

toolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);
```

# Adding a New Tool

Tools let the AI model fetch data or perform actions during a conversation. When the model decides it needs information (like weather data or a database lookup), it invokes a tool by name, the server executes it, and the result feeds back into the conversation.

Adding a new tool takes two steps: define it and register it. The rest is automatic -- the orchestrator passes tools to the AI provider, and the client already knows how to render any tool entry.

## Step 1: Create the tool file

Create a new file in `src/orchestration/tools/`. Each tool exports two things:

- A **`ToolDefinition`** describing the tool's name, purpose, and input schema
- A **`ToolExecutor`** function that runs the tool and returns a JSON string

Here is a complete example:

<!-- doc-block: example/weather-tool.ts#weather-tool -->
```typescript
import type {ToolDefinition, ToolExecutor} from '@re-cinq/hal-engine';

export const weatherTool: ToolDefinition = {
  name: 'get_weather',
  description:
    'Get the current weather for a location.\n\n' +
    'Use this tool when the user:\n' +
    '* Asks about weather or temperature\n' +
    '* Wants to know conditions at a specific place\n' +
    '* Needs a forecast for planning\n\n' +
    'Returns temperature, conditions, humidity, and wind speed.',
  promptInstructions:
    'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +
    'Call this for questions like "What is the weather in Berlin?" or "Is it raining in Tokyo?"',
  examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],
  inputSchema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties: {
      location: {
        type: 'string',
        description: 'The city name or location to look up.',
      },
      units: {
        type: 'string',
        enum: ['celsius', 'fahrenheit'],
        description: 'Temperature units. Defaults to celsius.',
      },
    },
    required: ['location'],
  },
};

export const executeWeather: ToolExecutor = async input => {
  // `input` has already passed the declared inputSchema; keys the schema does not declare can still be present.
  const result = {
    location: input.location as string,
    temperature: 18,
    units: input.units === 'fahrenheit' ? 'fahrenheit' : 'celsius',
    conditions: 'Partly cloudy',
    humidity: 65,
    windSpeed: 12,
    windUnit: 'km/h',
  };

  return JSON.stringify(result);
};
```

### Writing a good tool description

The `description` field is what the AI model reads to decide when to use the tool. Be specific:

- List the situations where the tool should be used ("Use this tool when...")
- Describe what the tool returns
- Give example queries if it helps

The more precise the description, the better the model's judgment about when to invoke it.

### Adding prompt instructions

The optional `promptInstructions` field provides guidance that gets included in the AI's system prompt. Unlike `description` (which is part of the tool schema sent to the AI provider), `promptInstructions` appears in the system prompt text itself, giving higher-level behavioral rules about when and how to use the tool.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
promptInstructions:
  'Use this when users ask about weather at a specific location. ' +
  'Call this for questions like "What is the weather in Berlin?" or "Is it raining in Tokyo?"',
```

The `ToolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` method collects these from all registered tools, and the `PromptBuilder` assembles them into the system prompt automatically. If you don't provide `promptInstructions`, the tool still works -- it just won't have explicit guidance in the system prompt.

Use `promptInstructions` for:
- Short, actionable rules about when to call the tool
- Critical behavioral constraints (e.g., "MUST call this for every weather question")
- Example queries that help the model match user intent

Don't duplicate what's already in `description` -- keep `promptInstructions` focused on behavioral rules rather than describing inputs/outputs.

### Adding example prompts

The optional `examplePrompts` field provides example queries that are shown to users in the chat interface as clickable suggestions. These are sent to the client in the WebSocket `connected` message and persist throughout the conversation.

<!-- doc-block: none -- one field of a ToolDefinition, quoted to discuss how to word it -->
```typescript
examplePrompts: ['What is the weather in Berlin?', 'Is it raining in Tokyo?'],
```

The `ToolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` method collects and flattens these from all registered tools. They are computed once at server startup and included in every new WebSocket connection's `connected` message.

Guidelines:
- Write prompts as natural user questions, not technical descriptions
- Keep them short and specific -- they appear as pill-shaped buttons in the UI
- 1-2 prompts per tool is enough; the total across all tools should stay manageable
- Use realistic terminology relevant to your application domain

### Defining the input schema

The `inputSchema` follows [JSON Schema](https://json-schema.org/) format. The model uses this to construct the correct input.

- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields
- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these
- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)

### Writing the executor

A `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

The optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.

- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message
- Cast input fields from `unknown` to their expected types
- Handle missing or unknown input gracefully (return a reasonable default or error message)

For tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.

## Step 2: Register the tool

Open `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:

<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->
```typescript
import {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';

// ... existing registrations ...

toolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);
```

That is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry looks up the executor by name and runs it.

## What happens automatically

Once a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:

**On the backend:**

- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider
- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`
- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`
- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)

**On the client:**

- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields
- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**
- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**
- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives

## File reference

| File | What it contains |
|------|-----------------|
| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |
| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |
| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |

The model uses this to construct the correct input, and the registry enforces it: a call that does not satisfy the schema never reaches your executor. The schema is a provider-facing hint in both directions -- `required`, declared types and `enum` are validated, and nothing else is added to the call (`additionalProperties` stays open, no coercion, no defaults).

- Use `required` to mark mandatory fields
- Add `description` to each property -- the model reads these
- Tool parameter names use `snake_case` (this is the convention from the AI provider API, wrap them in `/* eslint-disable camelcase */` comments)

A call the schema rejects is answered with a tool result naming what was wrong -- the missing required property, or the expected type of a mistyped field -- so the model reads it and corrects the call on its next round. The executor is not invoked for that call. See `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md` for the full contract.

### Writing the executor

A `ToolExecutor` is an async function that takes the tool input and returns either a string or a `ToolResponse`:

<!-- doc-block: src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts#ToolExecutor -->
```typescript
type ToolExecutor = (input: Record<string, unknown>, context?: ToolContext) => Promise<string | ToolResponse>;
```

The optional `context` provides `userId`, `sessionId`, `workspaceId`, and `authHeaders` for tools that need to make authenticated API calls.

- Return `JSON.stringify(result)` for most tools -- the result gets added to the conversation as a tool result message
- Input reaching your executor has already passed the declared schema: the declared fields are present and of the declared type, so read them directly instead of casting defensively or handling missing input
- Keys the schema does not declare can still be present -- the registry does not strip undeclared properties -- so ignore extras or read them as the `unknown` values they are

For tools that need to send messages directly to the client or suppress the AI's echo, return a `ToolResponse` object instead of a plain string. See [tool-responses.md](../specs/hal-engine-tool-responses/spec.md) for a full walkthrough.

## Step 2: Register the tool

Open `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` and add two lines:

<!-- doc-block: example/register-tool.ts#register -->
```typescript
import {weatherTool, executeWeather} from './weather-tool.js';

// ... existing registrations ...

toolRegistry.register(weatherTool, executeWeather);
```

That is it. The `ToolRegistry` feeds all registered tool definitions to the chat orchestrator, which passes them to the AI provider. When the model invokes the tool, the registry validates the call against the schema the tool declared -- compiling a static schema once at registration, so a broken schema fails at startup -- and only runs the executor for a call that passed.

## What happens automatically

Once a tool is registered, the following work without any additional code:

**On the backend:**

- `toolRegistry.getExamplePrompts()` collects example prompts from all tools and includes them in the WebSocket `connected` message
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getPromptInstructions()` to include tool guidance in the system prompt via `PromptBuilder`
- `chatOrchestrator.ts` calls `toolRegistry.getDefinitions()` to pass all tools to the AI provider
- When the provider returns a `tool_use` chunk, the message handler creates a `ToolEntry` and sends it via `entry_upsert`
- The orchestrator executes all pending tool calls in parallel with `Promise.all()`
- Tool results are added to the conversation, and the provider is re-queried (up to `maxToolRounds` rounds)

**On the client:**

- Tool entries can be rendered by the client using the `toolName` and `toolInput` fields
- `formatToolName()` strips common prefixes (`get_`, `calculate_`, `fetch_`, `find_`) and title-cases the remaining words. So `get_weather` becomes **Weather**
- `formatParamName()` converts `snake_case` parameter names to Title Case for display. So `wind_speed` becomes **Wind Speed**
- A spinner shows on the last tool entry until a subsequent entry arrives

## File reference

|------|-----------------|
| `src/types/ai.ts` | `ToolDefinition` interface (includes `promptInstructions`, `examplePrompts`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` | `ToolExecutor` type, `ToolResponse` interface, `ToolRegistry` class (includes `getPromptInstructions()`, `getExamplePrompts()`) |
| `src/orchestration/tools/index.ts` | Tool registration (add your import and `register()` call here) |
| `src/infrastructure/builders/promptBuilder.ts` | `PromptBuilder` class that assembles the system prompt from tool instructions |
| `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` | Where tools are passed to the provider and executed |
